options: The more you speak Turkish, the easier it gets.
Until you start speaking Turkish, it won't get easier.
The whole time you speak Turkish, it's easy.
items.explanation: -tukça is “the more / as.” The second half grows: daha kolay.

options: Unless you tap your card, the door won't open.
The more often you tap your card, the worse the door opens.
The door is open as long as you have a card.
items.explanation: -madıkça is “unless / until.” English has no “not” here, Turkish does: -ma-.

options: As long as you're here, you can stay with us.
The longer you're here, the less you can stay with us.
You can't stay with us until you stay.
items.explanation: -dığın sürece is “as long as you…”: word for word, “as long as your staying here.”

options: In summer I'm sometimes in Ankara.
The more summer there is, the more I'm in Ankara.
items.explanation: Boyunca is “throughout,” placed after the noun: yaz boyunca = all summer long.

items.translation: The more I read, the more I understand.
items.explanation: Oku: last vowel u, voiced ending — dukça.

items.translation: The more you speak, the easier it gets.
items.explanation: Ş is voiceless — t, like the t sound in “walked”; vowel u — tukça.

items.translation: The weather is getting colder and colder.
items.explanation: Git ends in t — voiceless, so tikçe: gittikçe.

items.translation: Unless you tap your card, the door won't open.
items.explanation: “Unless” in Turkish has a “not” inside: okut + ma + dıkça.

items.translation: As long as you're here, you can stay with us.
items.explanation: Before sürece — “your staying”: sen → kaldığın.

exercises.instruction: Match the beginning and the end.

items.explanation: Over time — you get used to it. Without the doctor's OK — no discharge. While you work — gloves. During the whole meeting — phones off. All night — no sleep.

exercises.instruction: Find the mistake and fix it.

items.explanation: After voiceless ş — t, like the t sound in “walked”: konuştukça.
“Throughout the summer” after a noun is boyunca. Sürece needs a verb with a person: -dığı sürece.
Kaldın is just “you stayed.” Before sürece you need “your staying”: kaldığın.
English “until it goes down” has no “not.” Turkish needs one: düş + me + dikçe.

exercises.instruction: Form analysis: from the sentence, figure out its graph — growing, until, as long as the condition holds, or the whole stretch.

items.explanation: -dukça: the more I read, the more I understand.
-medikçe: until they let you — you're not getting in.
-dığın sürece: as long as you're here — a condition.
Boyunca: the whole summer.
Geçtikçe: over time — growing.
-madıkça: unless you tap your card — closed.
-dığınız sürece: as long as you work — the rule applies.
Boyunca: the whole night.

items.statement: -DIkçA never takes person endings: not “kaldığımça,” but “kaldıkça.”
items.explanation: Yes. Person and tense are carried by the second half of the sentence.

items.prompt: How do you say “Until the results come in, I can't say anything”?
items.explanation: English “until” has no “not”; Turkish puts one inside: gel + me + dikçe. The second half is a “can't.”

items.prompt: “It rained all week” — which is right?
items.explanation: “All week” = noun + boyunca, in that order: hafta boyunca.

items.statement: “Çalıştıkça yoruluyorum” and “Çalıştığım sürece yoruluyorum” mean the same thing.
items.explanation: The first is “the more I work, the more tired I get” (growth). The second is “as long as I work” (condition).

items.prompt: “I'll wait until you come.” Which is right?
items.explanation: A plain time limit is -(y)AnA kadar. -madıkça needs a “no” after it: Sen gelmedikçe gitmem. Geldikçe is “every time you come.”
